text.p: International news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc on Tuesday reported a 17 percent rise in full-year profits for 1996 but warned it would be difficult to improve its underlying revenue growth rate this year.

Reuters reported 1996 pre-tax profits of 701 million pounds ($1.15 billion) for 1996 and a 20 percent rise in the total dividend to 11.75 pence per share after revenue grew by eight percent to 2.91 billion pounds.
But its shares tumbled to stand 28p lower at 614p after the results in heavy trading of over 13 million shares.
Chief executive Peter Job said in a statement that to gain critical mass Reuters had restructured its pricing to encourage conversions to its new 3000 range of products from the current 2000 series.
"This will make it difficult for the group to better the underlying revenue growth rate achieved in 1996," he said.
He said orders for the 3000 products which combine real-time and historic data were coming in faster than expected but installations were slower.
"Orders are proceeding faster than expected at 14,700 though installations, at 2,500, are slower," Job said.
The launch on schedule of the 3000 series was the company's major initiative in 1996.
Referring to the recent sharp appreciation in sterling, Job said "...a robust sterling would severely restrict prospects for reported revenue and earnings growth."
This was despite the fact that by end 1996 Reuters had unrecognised currency hedging gains of 35 million pounds relating to 1997.
However, Job said, "..the strength of the underlying business is expected to enable Reuters to maintain double digit dividend growth in 1997."
Reuters, which last year suspended plans to return cash to shareholders via a share buyback scheme, said it continued to monitor developments in this area.

Reuters attempts to reduce its cash pile via a buy back were thwarted last year when the British government altered its tax regulations linked to such schemes, making them less attractive to certain shareholders.
"We continue to monitor developments in this area for an appropriate method of returning cash while we concentrate our efforts on managing the business," Job said.

The company also announced that GLOBEX, its automated matching system for futures contracts built with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the MATIF futures exchange in France, was not likely to continue beyond 1998 as the original partners developed their own systems.
"This product has never been particularly successful and its closure will not produce any material impact on the company's results," Reuters said.
The company said its transactions businesses continued to be the fastest-growing product line, with revenue up 21 percent to 813 million pounds.
It said Instinet, its electronic equity broking service, had "...another excellent year growing 42 percent to 346 million pounds."
It added flat markets led to slower growth in foreign exchange dealing products, particularly in the second half. ($1=.6120 Pound)
